c.tagline: Vibrant coastal capital where history, highlife music and beach life meet.

taxi.color: yellow-fendered (yellow front wings/doors on a colored body)
taxi.fareNote: Most street taxis are unmetered; agree the fare with the driver before setting off. Ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt, Yango) show fixed in-app pricing and are generally more reliable.

emergency.note: 112 is a universal emergency number that can route to police, fire or ambulance; response times outside central Accra can be slow.

hood_landmark.East Legon: A&C Shopping Mall, East Legon, Accra

avoid.reason: Petty crime around Makola market and at night; caution on the beaches

hood_desc: Accra's liveliest strip centered on Oxford Street, packed with bars, restaurants, craft markets and nightlife within walking distance; suits first-time visitors and younger travelers.
A leafy, upscale enclave beside Kotoka International Airport with embassies, business hotels and quiet tree-lined streets; suits business travelers and anyone wanting quick airport access.

A sprawling modern suburb favored by expats and the diaspora, with malls, cafes and gated compounds spread over a wide area; best for longer stays and those comfortable relying on ride-hailing or a car.
Beachfront area anchored by Labadi Beach with resort-style hotels, pools and ocean views; suits travelers who prioritize beach access and resort amenities.
A quiet, green diplomatic and hospital district close to the city center with upscale hotels; suits visitors wanting a calm, central base near Independence Square.
lodging: Best Western Plus Accra Beach Hotel

water.note: Tap water is treated but contamination risk remains; use bottled or purified water.

transit.pay: Tro-tros and most local buses are pay-cash-to-the-conductor on board; the Aayalolo BRT uses a rechargeable smart card tapped at boarding; ride-hailing apps (Uber, Bolt, Yango) are paid via in-app card or cash to the driver.
transit.hours: Tro-tros and buses generally run roughly 5am-9pm with sparse service after dark; taxis and ride-hailing apps operate 24/7 and are the main night option.
transit.note: Accra has no metro or tram; getting around relies on tro-tros, limited BRT/bus lines, and taxis/ride-hailing, with traffic congestion a major factor.

airport.name: Kotoka International Airport (ACC)
airport.drive: 20-40 min to central Accra depending on traffic (can exceed 1 hr at rush hour)

transit.m: Metro Mass Transit bus (infrequent, ~45 min to city)

tip.r: Not traditionally expected, but 5-10% in restaurants without a service charge is appreciated; rounding up for taxis and small tips for hotel staff are common.

food.name: Jollof rice
food.desc: Ghana's smoky one-pot rice simmered in tomato, pepper and aromatics with chicken or fish - the dish behind the great jollof rivalry.

places.name: Buka Restaurant
places.note: Two-storey Ghanaian institution with a treehouse-feel upper deck; jollof, kelewele and grilled tilapia done properly.

places.name: Azmera Restaurant
places.note: Buffet-style Ghanaian spread; taste jollof, waakye and banku side by side in one sitting.

places.name: Asanka Local
places.note: Open-air local joint with charcoal grills; jollof with chicken and a cold Club lager after dark.

food.name: Waakye
food.desc: Rice and black-eyed peas steamed with millet leaves until russet, piled with shito, gari, spaghetti, egg and stew - Accra's breakfast king.

places.name: Auntie Muni's Waakye
places.note: Legendary morning-only queue; pick your toppings at the netted counter - shito, gari, wele and boiled egg.

places.name: Azmera Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down version of the street staple with stew, spaghetti and fish, for those wary of roadside stalls.

places.name: Makola Market waakye stalls
places.note: Vendors ladling waakye from dawn; cheapest and most authentic option, cash only, usually gone by noon.

food.name: Banku with grilled tilapia
food.desc: Sour fermented corn-and-cassava dough eaten by hand with whole charcoal-grilled tilapia and a fiery ground pepper-and-onion shito relish.

places.name: Duncan's
places.note: Long queues most nights for charcoal tilapia and banku with pepper - a rite of passage in Osu.

places.name: Asanka Local
places.note: Grills going all evening; whole tilapia, banku and shito on a shaded terrace with highlife playing.

places.name: Philipo's
places.note: Roadside-bar style spot known for generously garnished tilapia and a scorching pepper sauce.

food.name: Kelewele
food.desc: Ripe plantain cubes tossed in ginger, chilli and nutmeg then fried until caramelised - Accra's classic evening street snack, often bagged with peanuts.

places.name: Oxford Street night stalls
places.note: After-dark braziers along the strip; spiced plantain cubes bagged fresh with roasted groundnuts.

places.name: Buka Restaurant
places.note: Reliable sit-down kelewele as a starter, fried to order and properly gingery.

places.name: Chez Clarisse Mama Africa
places.note: West African kitchen serving kelewele and alloco alongside attieke and grilled fish.

food.name: Fufu with light soup
food.desc: Pounded cassava-and-plantain dumpling dropped into peppery tomato light soup or groundnut soup with goat, chicken or smoked fish.

places.name: The Chop Bar
places.note: Modern chop bar in Achimota Retail Centre; fufu, banku and soups in a clean air-conditioned room.

places.name: Buka Restaurant
places.note: Light soup, groundnut soup and kontomire with fufu, all pounded to order.

places.name: Azmera Restaurant
places.note: Wide soup selection with fufu and omotuo rice balls; popular with Ghanaian families on Sundays.

food.name: Red red
food.desc: Black-eyed peas stewed in red palm oil with tomato and chilli, served with sweet fried plantain and a dusting of gari.

places.name: Buka Restaurant
places.note: Vegetarian-friendly plate of bean stew and plantain that travellers order again and again.

places.name: Asanka Local
places.note: Homestyle red red with plenty of palm oil richness, good value beside the grills.

places.name: Chez Clarisse Mama Africa
places.note: Pan-West African menu where red red sits next to attieke and grilled fish.

food.name: Sobolo
food.desc: Chilled hibiscus infusion spiced with ginger, cloves and pineapple - Ghana's ubiquitous non-alcoholic cooler, sold from street coolers to smart bars.

places.name: Makola Market drink vendors
places.note: Bottled sobolo sold ice-cold by the roadside; the cheapest and most everyday version.

places.name: Buka Restaurant
places.note: House-made sobolo and asaana on the drinks list, a good pairing with the pepper-heavy dishes.

places.name: Bloombar
places.note: Cocktail bar that spins sobolo into spritzes and mixed drinks with Ghanaian bitters.

food.name: Palm wine and akpeteshie
food.desc: Milky, lightly fizzy sap tapped from palm trees, and akpeteshie, the fierce spirit distilled from it - now also the base of Accra bar cocktails.

places.name: Republic Bar & Grill
places.note: Tiny Osu institution famous for the Kokroko cocktail built on akpeteshie; live highlife spills into the street.

places.name: Asanka Local
places.note: Palm wine served by the calabash beside the grills whenever a fresh tapping comes in.

places.name: Bloombar
places.note: Leans on Ghanaian spirits and bitters; a good, safe first taste of akpeteshie.

landmarks: Independence Square (Black Star Square)
Ghana's monumental parade ground featuring the iconic Black Star Gate, a powerful symbol of the nation's 1957 independence and pan-African pride.
Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park & Mausoleum
A striking marble mausoleum and museum honoring Ghana's first president, set in landscaped gardens celebrating the nation's independence hero.
Osu Castle (Christiansborg Castle)
A whitewashed 17th-century fortress on the Atlantic coast, once a Danish trading post and seat of government, now steeped in colonial history.
Jamestown Lighthouse
A weathered red-and-white lighthouse towering over Accra's oldest fishing district, offering panoramic ocean views from its historic quarter.
Ussher Fort
A 17th-century Dutch-built coastal fort turned museum, showcasing colonial and slave-trade history within Jamestown's historic waterfront.
National Museum of Ghana
Ghana's premier museum, displaying archaeological treasures, royal regalia, and Kente textiles that trace the country's cultural heritage.
Holy Trinity Cathedral
Accra's oldest church, a graceful colonial-era Anglican cathedral whose bell tower has anchored the city's High Street skyline since the 1890s.
Labadi Beach
Accra's liveliest stretch of golden sand, buzzing with music, horseback rides, and street food, drawing locals and tourists for weekend relaxation.
Makola Market
A sprawling, chaotic open-air market packed with textiles, produce, and crafts, offering an immersive taste of everyday Accra commerce and color.
W.E.B. Du Bois Centre
The former home and burial site of civil rights icon W.E.B. Du Bois, honoring his legacy as a pan-African intellectual who settled in Ghana.

train.note: No usable intercity passenger train runs from Accra. Ghana's only revived passenger services are in the Western Region (the short Kojokrom-Sekondi-Takoradi line, relaunched April 2026); the new standard-gauge Tema-Mpakadan line near Accra was commissioned but was still not carrying scheduled passengers as of mid-2026. There is no online rail booking - use long-distance coaches instead.

bus.note: Intercity STC international coaches leave from the STC terminal at the Ministries/Tudu area of central Accra; book at the counter or via stcticketing.gov.gh. ABC Transport runs the coastal Accra-Lome-Cotonou-Lagos corridor. Carry your passport and CFA/Naira cash for the land borders.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferry from Accra; the ports of Tema and Takoradi are cargo only. Domestically, Volta Lake Transport Company runs a passenger boat up Lake Volta (Akosombo-Yeji).

half.name: Cape Coast
half.blurb: Historic Ghanaian coastal town known for its centuries-old fort and slave-trade heritage.

full.name: Lomé
full.blurb: Togo's coastal capital, known for bustling markets and breezy Atlantic beaches.

full.name: Kumasi
full.blurb: Historic heart of the Ashanti Kingdom known for its markets and royal traditions.

full.name: Takoradi
full.blurb: Ghanaian port city known for its harbor, beaches, and offshore oil industry.

full.name: Sekondi-Takoradi
full.blurb: Twin port city on Ghana's coast known for fishing, harbors, and oil industry growth.

full.name: Obuase
full.blurb: Ghanaian town known for its long history of gold mining.

full.name: Aflao
full.blurb: Border town in eastern Ghana known as a busy crossing point and trading hub with Togo.

full.name: Tafo
